title: When We Choose Each Other
subtitle: Stars Between the Strings · Chapter 36 of 40
content:
The string lights were crooked.

Somebody had left a folded request card on the stage marked *Greg Universe — Love Song*. There was no name, no signature, just a suggestion that he dedicate the last number to “the person who finally got him to settle down.”

He read it and made a face.

“Wow. They managed to insult my whole life in one sentence.”

“You could leave it out.”

“Definitely will. I like love songs. I also like not having strangers write my relationship status on a napkin.”

He tucked the card beneath the sound board, away from the public list. When Ellis came to ask about the event, he told her the performance was for the people who'd worked on the square. He could talk about music and the crew. He didn't need to provide a tidy story about being saved by romance.

I touched his wrist under the table.

“I know it's hard when people think being with me means you've given up being on the road.”

“Yeah.” He sighed. “I spent a lot of years running from stuff. Also a lot of years driving to places because I actually wanted to go there. Those aren't the same thing.”

“You don't have to prove you're settled by staying still.”

“Good, because the van would get suspicious.”

His grin came back unevenly. He drew me against his side long enough for me to hear his heartbeat beneath the ridiculous shirt he insisted was stage wear. I caught the smell of the ocean and the cinnamon frosting from the volunteers' cake.

“You look nervous,” I said.

“I'm about to sing in front of fifty people while you stand there looking at me like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like you already know how the song ends.”

I kissed him behind the sound board. It did not make the lights straighten or the band arrive, but it made the waiting a lot more interesting.

One loop dipped low enough to brush Greg's hair. Another had been wound around the same post three times because someone had changed their mind about where the party ought to end. The band was late, the paper plates were trying to escape in the wind, and Greg was standing in the middle of the Beach City square with a microphone he had no intention of using.

"You're staring," he said.

"I'm assessing the danger."

"The lights?"

"Your haircut."

He grinned and tucked a loose strand behind his ear.

The celebration had started as a small gathering after a community cleanup. People had carried away storm debris, repaired the picnic tables, and borrowed the church's folding chairs for the evening. Greg had volunteered music for one set; I had promised to help lay out the food. Neither of us had agreed to be the event's romantic headline.

Then a local newspaper had asked for a photograph.

The reporter, a young woman named Ellis, approached with a camera and a folded page of interview notes. She looked nervous.

"Greg, can I get one shot of you and Jasper? People have been talking about you two."

Greg's smile thinned, almost invisibly.

"Depends what the story's about," he said.

"The cleanup. And, well, the relationship. It's kind of sweet. Maybe a little unconventional."

I set down a stack of cups.

"Unconventional how?"

Ellis glanced at her notes.

"Someone said you travel a lot, Jasper. That you see other people."

Greg looked at me, not to make me answer but to check whether I wanted to.

"I do," I said. "I'm ethically non-monogamous and prefer polyamory. Everyone I'm involved with knows that, and each relationship is based on informed choice."

Ellis nodded quickly.

"So you aren't serious with Greg?"

My stomach dropped.

"That's not what I said."

She blushed.

"Sorry. I didn't mean—"

"I know. But I'd like you to ask what we actually mean instead of choosing a story where somebody must be temporary."

Greg exhaled.

"I was about to say something stupid," he admitted.

"What kind?"

"Something about being lucky to have whatever time you can spare for me."

I looked at him.

"Greg."

"I know. It sounds kind of selfless until you realize it makes me look like a guy standing around hoping you'll pick him."

Ellis lowered her camera.

"I can leave the relationship out of the article."

"That would be my preference," I said. "You can write about the cleanup. Ask the people who worked on the drainage ditch. Ask who hauled the chairs. Don't turn our private time into a test for strangers."

Ellis nodded.

Then she asked, "Can I photograph the repaired picnic table?"

"Please," I said.

She went to find the volunteers.

For a moment neither Greg nor I spoke. The wind lifted the napkins, and we had to chase them down the path in a ridiculous little scramble.

Greg caught the last one against his chest.

"Great start," he said.

"You're very dignified."

"I've been told."

We returned to the tables. He straightened the napkins while I tried to decide whether to bring up the line he'd almost said. I didn't want to leave it sitting between us like a broken instrument neither of us wished to touch.

"About being grateful for whatever time I can spare," I said.

He went still.

"I know."

"Do you actually feel that way?"

"Sometimes." He looked at his hands. "I don't want to make you smaller. I like that you have places to go and people to see. I also don't want to pretend I never miss you."

"Then tell me when you miss me. That's allowed."

"Is it?"

"Yes. I'm your partner, not a holiday rental."

He laughed, startled.

"Okay. That's fair."

I stepped closer.

"I choose you when I'm here. I also choose to be honest when I have plans elsewhere. Those aren't competing truths."

He set the stack of napkins down.

"And I can ask for time?"

"You can. I can say yes or no. You get to say no to me too."

He looked at me with an expression both embarrassed and intensely fond.

"Pretty sure I'm going to need practice."

"Me too."

Steven arrived carrying a cooler, rescued the conversation by tripping over a cable, and promptly asked why the band hadn't started yet.

"Artistic suspense," Greg said.

"You're not even playing yet."

"Exactly."

Steven shook his head and helped set the cooler down. He had brought enough cold drinks for the volunteers. Greg asked whether he wanted to stay for the music; Steven said yes, then went to help move chairs.

No one turned him into a witness to our romantic discussion.

A little later Ellis returned with the article draft. She had removed the guesses about our relationship and added the names of the volunteers who had repaired the square. She asked us to check our direct quotations before printing.

"Better," I said.

Greg smiled.

"Look, someone actually wrote about the storm drain. This town is growing up."

The band finally arrived. Their drummer apologized for being late; a delivery truck had blocked the road. Greg helped carry the cases but did not volunteer to manage the whole set. We hung the last string of lights high enough for people to walk beneath without ducking.

When the first song began, Greg reached for my hand.

"Want to dance?"

"I thought you'd never ask."

"I'm trying this new thing called asking."

"Very advanced."

He laughed and drew me into the uneven little space between the tables. We moved badly at first, bumping shoulders and laughing when the rhythm changed. He didn't pull me closer until I did, and when his thumb brushed my knuckles I felt the warmth of the choice we'd made in front of nobody who needed to know.

Across the square, the lights shone on the volunteers, the repaired tables, and the people eating too much cake. There was no grand declaration. We didn't ask the band to play a song about us.

Before we rejoined the crowd, Greg found a quiet place beside the stacked chairs where the music was just a muffled beat through the wall.

“You look nice,” he said.

“You've been looking at me all night.”

“Yeah, but I was trying to decide whether saying it would make me sound like a guy who just discovered compliments.”

“It might.”

He gave me an embarrassed grin. “Well, then. You look *really* nice.”

I put my palm against his chest. His shirt was warm from setting up amplifiers, and beneath it I felt the quick, startled rhythm of his breath. I liked that he wasn't always smooth. He'd spent years singing to strangers and could still be thrown off balance by one person standing too close.

“Can I kiss you?” I asked.

Greg's smile vanished for a second. Not because he didn't want it. Because he was listening.

“Yeah,” he said softly. “Please.”

I kissed him beneath the crooked string lights. He made a little noise of surprise when I touched the back of his neck, then rested both hands carefully at my waist. There was nothing dramatic about the way we stood together, and yet I could feel how much effort it cost him not to turn tenderness into a joke.

When we parted, he rested his forehead against mine.

“Uh,” he said. “I had a very cool thing to say.”

“Did you?”

“Completely gone. I think you broke the lead singer.”

“Can he be repaired?”

“Maybe. Might need another kiss. No promises about the warranty.”

I laughed against his cheek. We stayed another moment until Pilar called for a hand with the chairs. Greg asked if I wanted to return with him, and I did. Later we would close the curtains on the part of the evening that belonged to us. For now, he had volunteered for a cleanup shift, and I didn't mind watching him keep it.


When Greg kissed me, it was brief and sweet. I leaned against him, and he rested his cheek against my hair.

"Can we keep doing this?" he asked.

"The terrible dancing?"

"That, yes. But I meant being honest before I start making jokes instead."

I smiled.

"Let's practice."

We left the square after the cleanup shift we'd agreed to, not after every person had gone home. Steven promised to help the last volunteers collect the chairs. Ellis gave us a copy of the revised article, now mostly about the town's flood drains and the people who fixed them.

Greg tucked it under his arm.

At the van, he stopped and looked back at the crooked lights.

"Should we fix that loop?"

"Tomorrow."

"Really?"

"Really."

He kissed my cheek.

The next morning we returned with a ladder and a proper set of clips. The lights hung straight for exactly one afternoon before the sea breeze twisted one of them sideways again.

Greg looked up.

I looked at him.

We laughed.

The crooked loop stayed until the next scheduled repair, and our relationship did not depend on the entire town approving the shape of it.
